title: Looking under the lamp
hook: he lost his key inside the house but searches the street, because the light is better there

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diogenes throws away his cup, and week five closed. Your line was less to carry. Did you give the thing away? Day thirty-six, and a new week begins.
screen: `DIOGENES THROWS AWAY HIS CUP — LESS TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: Week six, and a new kind of teacher. Not an emperor or a philosopher. A fool. Or someone who looks like one. His name is Nasruddin. In Turkey he's Nasreddin Hodja; in Iran and Central Asia, Mulla Nasruddin. People have told short, funny stories about him for a long time, in many lands: at weddings, in coffee shops, to children at bedtime. Nobody knows for sure whether he was one real man. The stories belong to the people who tell them. Here's one.
screen: `A NEW KIND OF TEACHER: A FOOL.` → `TOLD IN MANY LANDS.` → `THE STORIES BELONG TO THE TELLERS.`

segments.voice: It's night. A neighbor finds Nasruddin on his hands and knees in the street, under a lamp, searching the ground. What have you lost, Mulla? My key, he says. So the neighbor gets down and helps. They search for a long time. Every stone, every crack. Nothing. Finally the neighbor asks: are you sure you dropped it here? Where exactly did you lose it? Oh, says Nasruddin, inside the house. The neighbor stares at him. Then why on earth are we looking out here? And Nasruddin says: because there's more light here. It's a joke, and you're allowed to laugh. That's how these stories work. First you laugh at the fool. Then, a few seconds later, it's easy to notice he might be you. It's a very human habit: looking for things where it's easy to look, not where they are. Scientists even have a name for it now: the streetlight effect, studying what's easy to measure instead of what matters. And people do it with bigger things than keys. Looking for peace in the next purchase, when the restlessness is somewhere inside. Looking for the fix to a relationship in a new city, when the trouble came along in the suitcase. Some Sufi teachers have told this tale as a picture of the soul, searching the bright outside world for something that was lost within. But the tale itself doesn't explain. Nasruddin stories rarely do. They just leave you standing in the street with the fool, both of you holding a very good lamp, and both of you knowing, now, where the key really is.
screen: `ON HIS KNEES UNDER A LAMP.` · `I LOST IT INSIDE THE HOUSE.` · `THERE'S MORE LIGHT HERE.` · `THE FOOL IS YOU.` · then, large: `SEARCH WHERE YOU LOST IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then think of something you've been searching for lately. Not a key: something bigger. Calm, confidence, a better night's sleep, a closer friendship. Ask honestly: where have I been looking? Under which lamp? Then ask: where did I actually lose it? Don't solve it. Just let the answer point toward the house. The bell holds the time.
Looking under the lamp. Nasruddin searches the street for a key he lost inside, because the light is better out there.
Your line: search where you lost it. Today, take one small step toward the real place: the conversation, the habit, the room inside the house. Day thirty-six.

howItsDone: Nasruddin stories are told aloud across Turkish, Persian and wider Muslim cultures, often as a joke followed by a quiet moment of recognition; some Sufi teachers use them as teaching tales.

original.note: Persian, Mulla Nasruddin: mulla is a title for a learned man. In Turkish he is Nasreddin Hoca (Hodja), from Persian khwaja, master.

trapdoor: what you thought: a silly joke about a man who can't find his keys.
what it means: we look where it's easy, not where the thing is.

what a scholar hears: Nasruddin tales circulate in Turkish, Persian, Arabic and Central Asian versions; in some tellings of this one he has lost a ring or a coin, and some Sufi teachers have read it as a teaching story.

notes: Nasruddin tales are traditional and paraphrased; no modern collection is quoted. Versions vary (in some, a ring or coin; in the 'streetlight effect' version, a drunk).
Whether Nasruddin was historical is debated; Turkish tradition places him in 13th-century Akşehir. Confirm phrasing.
Persian spelling ملا نصرالدین and Turkish Hoca < Persian khwāja; confirm.
The Sufi reading is attributed to 'some Sufi teachers' (popularized in the 20th century by Idries Shah, not named or quoted). A Muslim/Sufi Keeper may refine.
Nasruddin's culture is Muslim; the stories are told as folk humor, not scripture, and the script doesn't present them as religious teaching.
